analysis.one_liner: Lets student loan borrowers refinance federal and private student loans at lower fixed rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 36 senators behind it, it was sent to the Senate education committee on July 1, 2020 and received no further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let borrowers who took out federal student loans before July 2020 replace them with new loans at the lower interest rates in effect for the 2020-21 school year. It would also have created a new federal loan that pays off private student loans, giving those borrowers federal terms and access to federal repayment and forgiveness programs. It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers holding older federal student loans (Direct, FFEL, Perkins, and federal health-professions loans) who took them out before July 2020: the bill required the Education Secretary to swap those loans for new ones carrying the fixed rates set for the 2020-21 school year, without extending the repayment term [S3]. Borrowers with private student loans could apply for a new Federal Direct Refinanced Private Loan that pays off the private lender; the new loan would carry the undergraduate or graduate Direct loan rate and keep the same terms and benefits as a Direct Unsubsidized Stafford Loan, including eligibility for income-driven repayment and certain forgiveness and public-service repayment programs going forward [S3]. Refinanced-loan borrowers would get credit toward income-based repayment forgiveness for payments made on their original loans [S3]. The bill also required a public-awareness campaign and new reporting by private lenders on their loan volume and default rates [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Borrowers of older federal loans would be refinanced at the lower fixed rates set for the 2020-21 school year, replacing rates locked in when rates were higher, with no extension of their repayment term [S3].

Private student loan borrowers could refinance into a federal loan at the Direct Stafford rate, and the new loan would carry Direct-loan terms and benefits, including eligibility for income-based repayment and service-related repayment programs for balances and payments after refinancing [S3].
Payments made on original loans would count toward income-based repayment forgiveness on the refinanced loan, so borrowers near forgiveness would not lose progress [S3].

Private educational lenders would have to report loan volume, average rates, and default and delinquency data to the Education Department, Treasury, and the consumer protection bureau, and the Secretary would set eligibility rules to preclude lender windfall profits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would bear the difference between the old, higher rates and the new lower rates on refinanced federal loans, and would take private and FFEL loans onto the federal books by paying them off. Private lenders and holders of older guaranteed (FFEL) loans would lose the interest and servicing income on loans paid off under the program. Taxpayers ultimately absorb the cost of the lower-rate loans.

drawbacks.text: Refinancing carries a real federal cost: the government collects less interest on refinanced loans and pays off private and FFEL loans outright, and the bill includes no dedicated funding source or cost estimate [S3].

The benefit would flow mainly to people who attended or completed college, who on average earn more than those without degrees, so a fair objection is that taxpayer money spent on lower loan rates is not the most targeted form of relief.
Refinancing does not forgive debt; it lowers rates while preserving repayment terms, so borrowers still owe the full principal and accrued interest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the direct benefit is real: several points off the interest rate on a fixed-rate loan that keeps the same repayment term lowers lifetime payments. The honest cost is to the Treasury, which forgoes interest and takes on private loans, and the benefit distribution skews toward college graduates rather than the lowest-income households. As written, the bill was a straightforward rate-refinance program, not debt cancellation.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to its education committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 1, 2020, with 34 Democratic senators and one independent listed as original cosponsors [S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1].
The action history shows no further action: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
The bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, leaving the refinancing program uncreated [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders and holders of older guaranteed student loans kept the loans and interest income the bill would have moved off their books, and the federal government avoided the cost of refinancing at lower rates. Student loan borrowers got no change in their rates or terms.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 senators attached to the bill were Democrats plus one independent; no Republican cosponsored it, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have let borrowers pay off their private student loans with new federal loans at lower, fixed rates, draining the lenders' loan books of their highest-rate accounts. It would also have imposed new default and pricing disclosure rules and required the Secretary to write rules barring lender windfall profits [S3].

industries.industry: FFEL loan holders and guarantee agencies
industries.note: Older federally guaranteed (FFEL) loans would have been paid off and converted to Direct loans, ending the holders' interest and guarantee income on those loans. Holders would be paid in full, but their ongoing revenue stream would end [S3].

Converting FFEL and private loans to Direct loans would shift servicing volume toward Direct-loan servicers and away from servicers of older guaranteed loans, and the bill required FFEL servicers to notify borrowers about refinancing eligibility [S3].
